\section{Appendix-only calibrated response-locus corollaries and homogeneous level-set bookkeeping}\label{app:abstract-homogeneous-main}

The main response material contains one constant-lapse symmetry example for a
homogeneous spectral-weight profile in \Cref{prop:symmetry-homogeneous-main}.
It is not a derivation of the sampled kernels \(T_0,T_1\).  Everything
collected here is therefore only appendix-level algebra for one fixed
calibrated response function. No separate exact nonconstant-lapse UDW model
with
\[
\mathcal S_x(\Omega)\equiv\mathcal S(\Omega)
\]
is constructed here.

\begin{assumption}[Appendix-only homogeneous spectral-weight regime]\label{ass:homogeneous-spectral-main}
When the static response regularity and calibration of
\Cref{ass:kms-response-main} are imposed at a fixed gap $\Omega$ on a region
$U$, the homogeneous spectral-weight regime means
\[
\mathcal S_x(\Omega)\equiv\mathcal S(\Omega)>0\qquad(x\in U).
\]
This is a calibration hypothesis on the response model, not a consequence of
KMS detailed balance. In response-locus-pair statements it is used together with a
common scalar calibration, so that the same positive response amplitude
$\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\mathcal S(\Omega)$ enters the ideal-benchmark and
memory-transition source equations. It holds exactly at the amplitude level in
the symmetry model of \Cref{prop:symmetry-homogeneous-main}, although that
ultrastatic example has constant lapse and hence no nontrivial spatial
level-set geometry
by itself. Accordingly, any nonconstant-lapse homogeneous shell arguments below
are appendix-only calibrated level-set algebra for a fixed response function,
while \Cref{prop:spectral-stability-main,cor:asymptotic-horizon-main} record
the slow-variation substitute used when the shell pair is only asymptotically
homogeneous.
\end{assumption}

\begin{definition}[Appendix-only common-core response-locus data]\label{def:common-core-shell-data-main}
A response-locus pair is \emph{common-core} when the two records use the same
externally supplied scalar response calibration: gap, coupling scale, profile,
and state are fixed, while the counter mode is changed from
ideal one-step blanking to the sampled one-recovery-opportunity boundary-reset mode. A two-mode radius
record is a \emph{full common-core spatial level-set record} only when the
undivided response-locus equations recover one positive common response
amplitude for all ideal-benchmark and memory-transition members, the four radii
lie in the allowed exterior coordinate range of the background family, and the
regular codimension-one spatial level-set checks needed for shell language have
also been verified. The weaker ratio equations alone give only
ratio-admissible data.
\end{definition}

\subsection{Threshold-selected response loci for one fixed calibrated response function}

This subsection only inserts the two already selected record thresholds into
one prescribed calibrated response profile and then invokes
\Cref{thm:response-locus-main} for range and regularity.  No new detector
dynamics enter this appendix; every statement below is algebra inside the
already fixed function $R_\Omega$.  For the memory target the inverse-theorem
warning is part of the statement:
\[
\mu_{\Gamma,\kappa_{\mathrm r}}=\mu_{\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Gamma},
\qquad
\text{so the visible record identifies only }
\{e^{-\Gamma\Delta\tau},e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm r}\Delta\tau}\}.
\]
Thus \(R_\Omega(x)=\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau)\) is a labelled
response target only after \(\kappa_{\mathrm r}\) has been independently
labelled by scalar calibration, recovery measurement, or an
external experimental protocol.  Without this label the response statement is
only a quotient statement under
\((\Gamma,\kappa_{\mathrm r})\sim(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Gamma)\).
\Cref{conv:branch-map-labelled-rates-main} is the standing reporting
convention for any labelled-rate statement.
Even with the label, a finite click record from one setting supplies only the
fixed-setting record inference stated in \Cref{thm:one-record-estimates-main};
it does not locate this response locus or infer a shell.

\begin{corollary}[Conditional level-set insertion for the sampled-record thresholds]\label{thm:shells-general-main}
\ResponseStandingClause the two classical record thresholds
from \Cref{sec:records} lift to the following response loci for one fixed
stationary scalar response model. Fix
$(\Omega,\lambda_c,\Delta\tau,\kappa_{\mathrm r})$ in a static KMS background,
so that \Cref{ass:response-standing-main} supplies the gap-regular absolutely
continuous spectrum near $\pm\Omega$, the absence of atoms there, the
positivity of $\widehat W_x(\Omega)$, and the $C^1$ regularity of
$x\mapsto\mathcal S_x(\Omega)$ and $R_\Omega$ on the region of interest. For
that fixed response function $R_\Omega$, the two record benchmarks are
equivalent to the following response loci. Their
nonemptiness is exactly the range check
$\gamma_\varphi,\gamma_{\mathrm{mem}}\in\operatorname{range}(R_\Omega)$, and
spatial shell language applies only when a spatial profile has been specified
and at points where $dR_\Omega\neq 0$.  This corollary does not assert a
detector-dynamics theorem beyond the standing calibrated response input.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.2em,itemsep=0.25em]
\item The ideal one-step blanking counter mode reaches the Parry benchmark
exactly on the response locus
\begin{equation}\label{eq:shell-phi-general-main}
\Sigma_{\varphi}=
\left\{x:
\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\mathcal S_x(\Omega)\Delta\tau}{e^{\beta_\infty N(x)\Omega}-1}=\log\varphi
\right\}.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, this is the fixed-response locus $R_\Omega^{-1}(\gamma_\varphi)$.
Wherever a spatial profile has been specified and \(dR_\Omega\neq0\) on this
locus, \Cref{thm:response-locus-main} upgrades the corresponding component to
a smooth codimension-one spatial level set; otherwise it remains only a
response locus inside the chosen calibrated model.

\item The sampled one-recovery-opportunity boundary-reset counter mode reaches
the memory-transition point exactly on the response locus
\begin{equation}\label{eq:shell-mem-general-main}
\Sigma_{\mathrm{mem}}=
\left\{x:
\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\mathcal S_x(\Omega)}{e^{\beta_\infty N(x)\Omega}-1}
=\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau)
\right\}.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, this is the fixed-response locus
$R_\Omega^{-1}(\gamma_{\mathrm{mem}})$. Wherever a spatial profile has been
specified and \(dR_\Omega\neq0\) on this locus, the corresponding component is
a smooth codimension-one spatial level set. On the locus itself, the sampled
record is exact $1$-dependent.
\end{enumerate}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
For the ideal counter mode, Lemma~\ref{prop:ideal-main} says that the
Parry benchmark is equivalent to $\Gamma\Delta\tau=\log\varphi$. Under the
Model~A assumption of \Cref{ass:udw-rate-calibration-main}, this becomes
$R_\Omega(x)\Delta\tau=\log\varphi$, i.e. $R_\Omega(x)=\gamma_\varphi$ with
the standing shorthand from \eqref{eq:target-rates-main}. This condition is
exactly \eqref{eq:shell-phi-general-main}, so the locus is
$R_\Omega^{-1}(\gamma_\varphi)$. The range and regularity statements are then
exactly the content of \Cref{thm:response-locus-main}.

For the sampled one-recovery-opportunity boundary-reset model,
\Cref{thm:main-record-wrapper,lem:one-dep-criterion-main} say that the memory
transition is equivalent to $\Gamma=\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau)$
only after the recovery rate has been independently labelled.  The visible
record itself obeys
\(\mu_{\Gamma,\kappa_{\mathrm r}}=\mu_{\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Gamma}\) and
identifies only
\(\{e^{-\Gamma\Delta\tau},e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm r}\Delta\tau}\}\), so without
that label the memory transition is a quotient statement, under the reporting
convention in \Cref{conv:branch-map-labelled-rates-main}.
Under the same Model~A assumption, this becomes
$R_\Omega(x)=\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau)$, i.e.
$R_\Omega(x)=\gamma_{\mathrm{mem}}$. With the same fixed calibrated response
function, this is exactly \eqref{eq:shell-mem-general-main}, so the locus is
$R_\Omega^{-1}(\gamma_{\mathrm{mem}})$. Every point satisfying that equation
has an exact $1$-dependent sampled record in that model. The
\Cref{lem:one-gap-kms-underdetermination-main} explains why this corollary is
only conditional on one fixed calibrated response function: changing
$\mathcal S_x(\Omega)$ changes the loci while preserving one-gap detailed
balance.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Homogeneous specialization of the fixed calibrated response theorem}

No new detector-field input is added below. The remaining statements start from
\Cref{thm:response-locus-main,thm:shells-general-main} and then impose extra
calibration or background hypotheses in the one-way order
\[
\text{fixed }R_\Omega
\Longrightarrow
\text{response loci}
\Longrightarrow
\text{pair transport}
\Longrightarrow
\text{homogeneous toy-model specializations}.
\]
Any nonconstant lapse is inserted only at the last stage of that chain.

\begin{lemma}[Abstract calibrated toy-model corollary: homogeneous specialization]\label{lem:abstract-homogeneous-specialization-main}
\ResponseStandingClause specialize the fixed calibrated response function $R_\Omega$ to the homogeneous form
below. Fix a static region $U$, a gap $\Omega>0$, a Tolman parameter
$\beta_\infty>0$, a positive constant \(\mathcal A\), and a $C^1$ lapse
$N:U\to(0,\infty)$. Define the calibrated response function
\[
R_\Omega^{\mathrm{hom}}(x)=\frac{\mathcal A}{e^{\beta_\infty N(x)\Omega}-1}.
\]
Then for any target rate $\gamma>0$ the response locus
\[
L_\gamma^{\mathrm{hom}}
=\{x\in U:R_\Omega^{\mathrm{hom}}(x)=\gamma\}
\]
is exactly the lapse level set
\[
\beta_\infty N(x)=\frac{1}{\Omega}\log\!\left(1+\frac{\mathcal A}{\gamma}\right).
\]
If $dN(x_0)\neq0$ at $x_0\in L_\gamma^{\mathrm{hom}}$, then
$L_\gamma^{\mathrm{hom}}$ is near $x_0$ a $C^1$ codimension-one spatial level
set. This is
an abstract calibrated toy-model specialization of a fixed response function.
The only profile-supporting example used here is
\Cref{prop:symmetry-homogeneous-main}, where the lapse is constant; whenever
later appendices use homogeneous nonconstant-lapse spatial level-set geometry,
they do so through this level-set specialization rather than through a separate
exact UDW construction or a derivation of the sampled kernels.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Solving $R_\Omega^{\mathrm{hom}}(x)=\gamma$ gives
\[
e^{\beta_\infty N(x)\Omega}=1+\frac{\mathcal A}{\gamma},
\]
hence the displayed lapse level set. Differentiating yields
\[
dR_\Omega^{\mathrm{hom}}
=-\mathcal A\frac{\beta_\infty\Omega e^{\beta_\infty N\Omega}}
{(e^{\beta_\infty N\Omega}-1)^2}\,dN,
\]
whose scalar prefactor is strictly negative. Therefore
$dR_\Omega^{\mathrm{hom}}(x_0)\neq 0$ exactly when $dN(x_0)\neq0$, and the
regular level-set theorem gives the spatial level-set statement.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Abstract calibrated toy-model corollary: homogeneous lapse-level sets]\label{cor:homogeneous-main}
\ResponseStandingClause assume in addition the calibrated homogeneous spectral-weight regime.
Assume in addition that $\mathcal S_x(\Omega)\equiv\mathcal S(\Omega)$ on the
region under study. Then both response loci are pure lapse level sets, with local inverse
temperatures
\begin{equation}\label{eq:betaphi-betamem-main}
\beta_{\varphi}=
\frac{1}{\Omega}
\log\!\left(1+\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\mathcal S(\Omega)\Delta\tau}{\log\varphi}\right),
\qquad
\beta_{\mathrm{mem}}=
\frac{1}{\Omega}
\log\!\left(1+\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\mathcal S(\Omega)}
{\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau)}\right),
\end{equation}
so that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:lapse-level-main}
\Sigma_{\varphi}=\{x:\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}(x)=\beta_{\varphi}\},
\qquad
\Sigma_{\mathrm{mem}}=\{x:\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}(x)=\beta_{\mathrm{mem}}\}.
\end{equation}
If $dN\neq0$ on one of these level sets, then
\Cref{thm:response-locus-main,lem:abstract-homogeneous-specialization-main}
identify it as the corresponding regular spatial level set; for nonconstant lapse this remains an
abstract calibrated toy-model specialization.
No companion homogeneous spatial theorem is invoked here: the conclusion is only
the regular level-set theorem applied to the displayed homogeneous response
function.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
With $\mathcal S_x(\Omega)\equiv\mathcal S(\Omega)$, the two response-locus
equations contain $x$ only through $\beta_\infty N(x)$. Solving the
ideal-benchmark equation for $\beta_\infty N(x)$ gives $\beta_\varphi$, and
solving the memory equation gives $\beta_{\mathrm{mem}}$. Hence the loci are
the lapse level sets in~\eqref{eq:lapse-level-main}.
\end{proof}

For later pair comparisons write $r_\varphi$ and
$r_{\mathrm{mem}}$ for the homogeneous ideal-benchmark and
memory-transition radii, and set
\[
D_\varphi=e^{\beta_\infty\Omega N(r_\varphi)}-1,
\qquad
D_{\mathrm{mem}}=e^{\beta_\infty\Omega N(r_{\mathrm{mem}})}-1,
\qquad
Q_{\varphi/\mathrm{mem}}=\frac{D_\varphi}{D_{\mathrm{mem}}}.
\]
The target-rate quotient used later is recorded in \Cref{thm:ratio-main}; here
we use only the level-set formulas above.

\subsection{Monotone spherical lapse bookkeeping in the abstract calibrated toy model}

Everything here stays at the level of
\Cref{lem:abstract-homogeneous-specialization-main}. No new exact
detector-field realization with
$\mathcal S_x(\Omega)\equiv\mathcal S(\Omega)$ is being claimed here.
Any nonconstant-lapse insertion is only bookkeeping for a fixed calibrated
response function.

\begin{proposition}[Abstract calibrated toy-model corollary: monotone spherical existence]\label{prop:existence-main}
\ResponseStandingClause assume in addition the homogeneous
specialization on a monotone spherical region.
Assume the homogeneous specialization of \Cref{cor:homogeneous-main} in a static
spherically symmetric region $r\in I$. Suppose
$N:I\to N(I)$ is $C^1$ and strictly monotone. For either threshold
$\star\in\{\varphi,\mathrm{mem}\}$, the corresponding response locus exists in $I$ if
and only if
\[
\frac{\beta_\star}{\beta_\infty}\in N(I),
\]
where $\beta_\varphi$ and $\beta_{\mathrm{mem}}$ are defined in~\eqref{eq:betaphi-betamem-main}. When it exists, its radius is unique and equals
\[
r_\star=N^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\beta_\star}{\beta_\infty}\right).
\]
If $N'(r_\star)\neq0$, this response locus is a regular spherical spatial
level set inside the abstract calibrated toy model.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By \Cref{cor:homogeneous-main}, the response-locus equation is exactly
$\beta_\infty N(r)=\beta_\star$. Since $N$ is strictly monotone on $I$, it is
one-to-one onto its range. Hence the equation has a solution precisely when
$\beta_\star/\beta_\infty$ lies in $N(I)$, and the solution is then the
displayed inverse image. Thus response-locus existence on a monotone spherical region is
completely equivalent to the calibrated target lapse lying in the available
range of $N$. The nonzero derivative condition is the one-dimensional form of
the regular level-set condition.
\end{proof}

Under this homogeneous specialization, both response loci are lapse level sets
selected by the two record thresholds and become spatial shells only after the
spatial profile, range, and regular level-set checks for the supplied response
function have all been supplied externally.  No finite record in this paper
estimates, locates, or supplies a confidence set for those loci. The default
comparison remains the transport identity
\Cref{cor:spectral-transport-main}; Appendix~\ref{app:schwarzschild-toy}
records a further Schwarzschild-lapse toy specialization.

\begin{proposition}[Abstract calibrated toy-model corollary: threshold-controlled ordering]\label{prop:order-main}
\ResponseStandingClause assume in addition the homogeneous
specialization. Assume the calibrated
homogeneous spectral-weight regime, and define
\[
\Gamma_{\varphi}=\frac{\log\varphi}{\Delta\tau}.
\]
Let $N_{\varphi}$ and $N_{\mathrm{mem}}$ denote the lapse values of the two
response loci $\Sigma_{\varphi}$ and $\Sigma_{\mathrm{mem}}$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:order-main}
N_{\varphi}<N_{\mathrm{mem}}
\iff
\Gamma_{\varphi}>\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau),
\end{equation}
with equality if and only if $\Gamma_{\varphi}=\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau)$. Thus the ordering of the two homogeneous response loci is controlled by the two supplied record thresholds; when a spatial profile and the regularity condition are both present, this is the corresponding spatial-level-set ordering inside the abstract calibrated toy model.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Both response loci are lapse level sets in the calibrated homogeneous
spectral-weight regime. Writing
\(\mathcal A=\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\mathcal S(\Omega)>0\),
the local excitation rate as a function of the lapse is
\[
\Gamma_+(N)=\frac{\mathcal A}{e^{\beta_\infty\Omega N}-1}.
\]
For $\beta_\infty,\Omega,N>0$,
\[
\frac{d\Gamma_+}{dN}
=
-\mathcal A\,\frac{\beta_\infty\Omega e^{\beta_\infty\Omega N}}
{(e^{\beta_\infty\Omega N}-1)^2}<0 .
\]
Hence the higher threshold rate corresponds exactly to the smaller lapse value, giving~\eqref{eq:order-main} and the equality statement.
\end{proof}

\mathtt{1670.735911330410671874886923646482926871711535334531094991}\\
&\mathtt{40719507619345342730084457122912},\\
q^+={}&
\mathtt{1670.735911330410671874886923646482926871711535334531094991}\\
&\mathtt{40719507619345342730665040208861}.
\end{aligned}
\]
}

\begin{lemma}[Certified population full-rank branch at \(z=1/2\)]\label{lem:z-half-diagonal-branch-certificate-main}
Let
\[
z=\frac12,\qquad \theta=\log2,\qquad
g_0=\frac{1-\log2}{2},\qquad g_1=\frac14,
\]
\[
\mu=2+2\log2,\qquad m_2=g_1+g_0^2 .
\]
Evaluate the displayed finite matrices \(A_z,B_z,e_z,d_z\) and the Jacobian
\(D\Phi(r(z))\) by the directed interval arithmetic transcript in
\Cref{tab:diagonal-branch-transcript-main}, with
rounding mode \(R\) equal to downward rounding for lower endpoints and upward
rounding for upper endpoints, and precision \(P=90\) significant decimal
digits.  The supplementary material gives the machine replay of this
population branch transcript, including the exact JSON transcript and
environment.  Those replay files support the printed interval arithmetic only.
The resulting enclosure for
\[
\Sigma_\sigma(1/2)
=D\Phi(r(1/2))\Sigma_r(1/2)D\Phi(r(1/2))^\top
\]
satisfies
\[
\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_\sigma(1/2)
\in[36.95298777813731,36.95298777813732],
\]
\[
\det\Sigma_\sigma(1/2)
\in[1.372485374000321,1.372485374000322].
\]
Therefore \(z=1/2\) belongs to the certified domain \(Z_{\rm cert}\), and the
certified population branch at this candidate is the full-rank branch:
\[
\operatorname{rank}\Sigma_\sigma(1/2)=2,qquad
\lambda_{\min}\{\Sigma_\sigma(1/2)\}>0.037.
\]
This certificate supplies only the covariance input used by Theorem~E's
pointwise projection example.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The preceding transcript is an outward-rounded directed interval evaluation of
the finite D-MAP covariance and quotient-sandwich formulas, with the exact
input singleton \([z]=[0.5,0.5]\).  Directed outward rounding at every
arithmetic operation ensures that the determinant enclosure contains the true determinant
\(\det\Sigma_\sigma(1/2)\).  Its lower endpoint is larger than \(1.37\), and
therefore
\[
[I_{\det}]\subset[1.37,\infty).
\]
Thus both eigenvalues are positive.  Moreover, for a positive definite
\(2\times2\) matrix,
\[
\lambda_{\min}=\frac{\det\Sigma_\sigma}{\lambda_{\max}}
\ge\frac{\det\Sigma_\sigma}{\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_\sigma}
>\frac{1.372485374000321}{36.95298777813732}>0.037.
\]
This gives the asserted rank and quantitative nondegeneracy.  Since the transcript is attached
only to the singleton input interval, it certifies no candidate other than
\(z=1/2\).  There is therefore no terminal subinterval list for a continuum
\(Z_{\rm cert}\) in this appendix; any later interval-valued certified domain
would have to print its terminal subintervals and margins separately.
\end{proof}


 succeeded in 227ms:
\section{Conditional UDW-rate calibration and fixed-response loci}\label{sec:kms-shells}

\newcommand{\ModelAClause}{Under Model A (\Cref{ass:udw-rate-calibration-main}), }
\newcommand{\ResponseStandingClause}{Under Model A and the standing response-side hypotheses of \Cref{ass:response-standing-main}, }

The record theory contributes two selected rates,
\[
\gamma_\varphi=\frac{\log\varphi}{\Delta\tau},
\qquad
\gamma_{\mathrm{mem}}=\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau),
\]
and this section inserts them into one fixed calibrated response function
$R_\Omega$. Sections~2--3 contain the main classical-counter results;
this section is only the shorter conditional response-side lift. Its output is
one fixed-response locus theorem for that prescribed $R_\Omega$. The UDW and KMS
facts recalled below are used only to define the possible calibrated profile and
to delimit what detailed balance does not determine. They do not derive the
classical sampled HMM.

\begin{corollary}[Boxed conditional calibration bridge from the classical counter to response loci]\label{cor:conditional-calibration-bridge-main}
\leavevmode\par\smallskip
\noindent\fbox{%
\parbox{\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax}{%
Suppose a stationary detector response calculation may motivate, and the
calibration protocol externally supplies, one positive $C^1$ scalar
excitation-rate profile
\[
R_\Omega(x)=\Gamma_+(x,\Omega)
\]
on a static region $U$, and suppose the sampled counter of
\Cref{sec:records} is calibrated only by the closure
\[
\Gamma=R_\Omega(x).
\]
Then the two classical counter conditions
\[
\Gamma=\gamma_\varphi,\qquad \Gamma=\gamma_{\mathrm{mem}}
\]
become only the response loci
\[
R_\Omega^{-1}(\gamma_\varphi),\qquad
R_\Omega^{-1}(\gamma_{\mathrm{mem}}).
\]
They become shell statements only after the target lies in the range of
$R_\Omega$ and $dR_\Omega\neq 0$ on the relevant level set. No converse is
asserted: KMS detailed balance or Tolman scaling alone does not produce the
sampled counter, the record law, or the response loci.
}}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
\Cref{prop:ideal-main} gives the ideal-counter condition
$\Gamma\Delta\tau=\log\varphi$, equivalently
$\Gamma=\gamma_\varphi$. \Cref{thm:main-record-wrapper,lem:one-dep-criterion-main}
give the sampled boundary-reset memory condition
$\Gamma=\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau)
=\gamma_{\mathrm{mem}}$. Substituting the calibration closure
$\Gamma=R_\Omega(x)$ gives the two displayed inverse images. The range and
regularity clauses are exactly the ordinary regular-level-set conditions later
formalized in \Cref{thm:response-locus-main}; they are not detector-dynamics
consequences.  Labelled-rate reporting follows
\Cref{conv:branch-map-labelled-rates-main}.
\end{proof}

The threshold-specific response-locus corollaries and the later homogeneous
toy-model specializations are collected in the appendices. Shell language is
used only when the target lies in the range of $R_\Omega$ and the regularity
condition $dR_\Omega\neq 0$ is verified. Appendix
Table~\ref{tab:hypothesis-ledger} collects the standing response-side
hypotheses, so the prose here records only the response-theoretic input not
already fixed by the stochastic analysis. From this point onward we also follow
\Cref{rem:notation-layers-main}: the record shorthands $p$, $s$, and
$\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}$ stay in \Cref{sec:records}, while the response layer
uses $\Gamma_\pm$, $\beta_\infty$, $\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}$, $\lambda_c$, and
$\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}$. Table~\ref{tab:notation-global} separates these
response-side symbols from the record-side and finite-kernel notation reused
most often from this point on.
The response-side contract is fixed once and for all by the boxed Model~A
assumption below. The response calculations in this section use that contract
only to insert the record-selected target rates into one chosen stationary
response profile; they do not derive the sampled instrument from UDW
measurement theory.

\paragraph{Logical order for the response-side material.}
The response-side material is a conditional corollary chain rather than a new
detector-dynamics theory.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.2em,itemsep=0.25em]
\item \Cref{prop:stationary-udw-response-main,lem:local-kms-spectral-main}
record the standard stationary UDW input at one fixed gap and extract one fixed
calibrated response profile $R_\Omega$.
\item \Cref{lem:one-gap-kms-underdetermination-main} shows that Tolman scaling
and one-gap KMS detailed balance do not determine the positive excitation
profile, so the calibrated $R_\Omega$ must be specified independently.
\item \Cref{thm:response-locus-main} is the central response-side proposition: once
$R_\Omega$ is fixed, the record-selected targets $\gamma_\varphi$ and
$\gamma_{\mathrm{mem}}$ become admissible response targets, and shell language
for the corresponding level sets is justified only after the separate range and
regularity checks.
\item Appendix~\ref{app:abstract-homogeneous-main} then packages the actual
target substitutions as conditional corollaries of that proposition.
\item Every later homogeneous, near-horizon, and fixed-radius inverse
statement is an additional algebraic specialization of that fixed-response
proposition, or of the pair transport law
\Cref{cor:spectral-transport-main}; none of those later statements is a new
exact nonconstant-lapse detector theorem. They are collected separately in the
abstract calibrated toy-model Appendices~\ref{app:abstract-homogeneous-main}
and~\ref{sec:inverse}, together with Appendix~\ref{app:schwarzschild-toy}.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Standing convention for this response section.}
Unless a later statement explicitly adds further input, the response-side
results in this section use Model~A together with the standing hypothesis
package recorded in \Cref{ass:response-standing-main}: the switched stationary
UDW input is gap-regular and absolutely continuous at $\pm\Omega$ with no atom
there, $\widehat W_x(\Omega)>0$, and the calibrated spectral weight
$x\mapsto\mathcal S_x(\Omega)$ is $C^1$ on the region under study, hence so is
$R_\Omega$. Appendix Table~\ref{tab:hypothesis-ledger} remains the ledger for
how those hypotheses are reused later. The result statements below restate only
the extra hypotheses that change the
conclusion.

\paragraph{Comparator boundary for the response-locus proposition.}
The response-locus family proved in this section is narrower than the recent
stationary-trajectory classification theorem of Bunney
\cite{Bunney2024StationaryTraj}. Bunney classifies stationary worldlines. Here
the stationary worldline, the stationary detector-response formula, and the
gap-regular response input are all fixed first, and the mathematical step is
then only target-rate level-set algebra for one calibrated response function
$R_\Omega$. The increment is therefore a conditional response-locus proposition,
with shell language added only after the range and regularity checks of
\Cref{thm:response-locus-main}. This also keeps the result on the response
side of the measurement-theory boundary surveyed by Papageorgiou--Fraser
\cite{PapageorgiouFraser2024LocalMeasurement}: no local QFT measurement
scheme, state-update rule, or detector-induced field observable is derived
from the sampled counter law.

Let $N(x)$ be the lapse function of a static spacetime and assume the field is in a global $\beta_\infty$-KMS state for Killing time. Along a static worldline at position $x$, Tolman scaling gives \cite{Tolman1930,TolmanEhrenfest1930}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tolman-main}
\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}(x)=\beta_\infty N(x).
\end{equation}
This relation fixes the proper-time KMS parameter seen by a static detector. It does not say that every local response observable is a function of $N(x)$ alone; mode density, boundary conditions, detector profile, and greybody transmission can still enter the absolute transition rate.

For a static worldline, the weak-coupling transition rates are Fourier transforms of the pulled-back two-point function. We use this standard UDW response fact explicitly rather than absorbing it into a response ansatz. Let $\Phi_x(\tau)$ denote the field operator smeared with the detector profile and transported along the static orbit through $x$, and set
\[
W_x(s)=\omega\!\left(\Phi_x(\tau)\Phi_x(\tau-s)\right),
\qquad
\widehat W_x(\nu)=\int_{\RR}e^{-i\nu s}W_x(s)\,ds,
\]
with the Fourier transform understood distributionally whenever $W_x$ is not an $L^1$ function.
Because $W_x$ is of positive type, its Fourier transform is represented by a
positive tempered measure $\mu_x$:
\[
\langle \widehat W_x,\phi\rangle=\int_{\RR}\phi(\nu)\,d\mu_x(\nu)
\qquad (\phi\in\mathcal S(\RR)).
\]
The response results below use only local gap regularity: there are open
neighborhoods of $\pm\Omega$ on which
\[
d\mu_x(\nu)=\widehat W_x(\nu)\,d\nu
\]
with $\widehat W_x$ finite and continuous. Equivalently, the spectral measure
has no atomic or singular component at either gap frequency.
The response-side input is therefore the standard stationary detector setup
rather than a new regularization scheme: stationary trajectories in the sense of
Letaw \cite{Letaw1981}, finite-size or smooth-switching regularizations in the
sense of Schlicht, Satz, and Louko--Satz
\cite{Schlicht2004,Satz2007,LoukoSatz2006,LoukoSatz2008}, and then the local
gap evaluation needed for the fixed calibrated response profile used below.

\begin{assumption}[Standard switched stationary response input, gap-regular spectrum, and KMS strip regularity]\label{ass:long-time-switch-main}
Fix a static worldline through $x$, a detector gap $\Omega>0$, and a smooth nonnegative switching profile $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ with $\int_{\RR}\chi=1$. Let $\chi_T(t)=\chi(t/T)$ and let $H_{g\to e}^{(T)}(x,\Omega)$ and $H_{e\to g}^{(T)}(x,\Omega)$ be the corresponding first-order transition probabilities for a detector with fixed spatial profile and bare coupling $\lambda_c$. Assume:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.2em,itemsep=0.25em]
\item The pullback $W_x$ is a tempered distribution on $\RR$, and there is an open interval $I_x\subset\RR$ containing $\pm\Omega$ and a continuous finite function, still denoted $\widehat W_x:I_x\to[0,\infty)$, such that the restriction of the spectral distribution to $I_x$ is the absolutely continuous measure $\widehat W_x(\nu)\,d\nu$. Equivalently, near $\pm\Omega$ the pulled-back spectrum is absolutely continuous with continuous density $\widehat W_x$, so there is no singular part and in particular no spectral atom at either $\pm\Omega$.
\item The switched first-order transition probabilities are given by the standard stationary UDW response pairing, with the finite-size/smooth-switching normalization used in the stationary detector literature \cite[Sec.~III]{LoukoSatz2006} and \cite[Sec.~II]{LoukoSatz2008}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:switched-pairing-main}
H_{g\to e}^{(T)}(x,\Omega)
=\lambda_c^2\langle W_x,K_{T,\Omega}\rangle,
\qquad
H_{e\to g}^{(T)}(x,\Omega)
=\lambda_c^2\langle W_x,K_{T,-\Omega}\rangle,
\end{equation}
where
\[
K_{T,\omega}(s)=e^{-i\omega s}\int_{\RR}\chi_T(u)\chi_T(u-s)\,du.
\]
Equivalently, whenever $W_x$ is represented by a function, this is the usual double integral
\begin{equation}\label{eq:switched-double-integral-main}
H_{g\to e}^{(T)}(x,\Omega)
=\lambda_c^2\int_{\RR^2}
\chi_T(\tau)\chi_T(\tau')e^{-i\Omega(\tau-\tau')}W_x(\tau-\tau')\,d\tau\,d\tau',
\end{equation}
with the de-excitation formula obtained by replacing $\Omega$ by $-\Omega$.
\item If the state is $\beta_\infty$-KMS with respect to static Killing time, then with $\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}(x)=\beta_\infty N(x)$ the usual KMS analyticity theorem for correlation functions supplies a function $F_x$ holomorphic on the strip \cite{HaagHugenholtzWinnink1967,KayWald1991,BratteliRobinson1997}
\[
S_{\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}}^-=\{z\in\mathbb C:-\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}(x)<\Im z<0\}
\]
such that for every closed substrip $-\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}(x)+\delta\le \Im z\le -\delta$ there exist $m_\delta\in\mathbb N$ and $C_\delta>0$ with
\[
|F_x(z)|\le C_\delta(1+|\Re z|)^{m_\delta},
\]
and the boundary values satisfy
\[
\lim_{\epsilon\to0^+}F_x(s-i\epsilon)=W_x(s),\qquad
\lim_{\epsilon\to0^+}F_x(s-i\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}(x)+i\epsilon)=W_x(-s)
\]
in $\mathcal S'(\RR)$.
\end{enumerate}
Define the switched effective coupling\footnote{The original bare coupling is $\lambda_c$; the switching convention contributes the fixed factor $\|\chi\|_2^2:=\int_{\mathbb R}\chi(u)^2\,du>0$.} by
\[
\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2:=\lambda_c^2\,\|\chi\|_2^2
\]
and use $\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}$ in the long-time rate formulas below.
\end{assumption}

\begin{lemma}[Approximate identity used to adapt the standard stationary response formula]\label{lem:gap-regular-approx-identity-main}
Fix $\omega\in\RR$ and define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:approx-identity-main}
\Phi_{T,\omega}(\nu)=
\frac{T}{2\pi\|\chi\|_2^2}\,
\bigl|\widehat\chi\bigl(T(\omega-\nu)\bigr)\bigr|^2 .
\end{equation}
Then $\Phi_{T,\omega}$ is a nonnegative approximate identity centered at
$\omega$. If $\mu$ is a positive tempered measure on $\RR$ and there is an open
interval $I\ni\omega$ together with a continuous finite density $f:I\to[0,\infty)$
such that
\[
\mu|_I=f(\nu)\,d\nu,
\]
then
\[
\langle \mu,\Phi_{T,\omega}\rangle\longrightarrow f(\omega)
\qquad (T\to\infty).
\]
Equivalently, the switched kernel extracts the absolutely continuous density at
the gap provided there is no spectral atom or singular part in a neighborhood of
$\omega$. This is the local analytic normalization needed to translate the
standard switched stationary UDW response formula of
\cite[Sec.~II]{LoukoSatz2008} into the Fourier convention, switching scale, and
gap-regular spectral-density boundary-value convention used in this paper; it
is not a new detector-response result.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The functions $\Phi_{T,\omega}$ are nonnegative and
\[
\int_{\RR}\Phi_{T,\omega}(\nu)\,d\nu
=\frac{1}{2\pi\|\chi\|_2^2}\int_{\RR}|\widehat\chi(\zeta)|^2\,d\zeta
=1
\]
by the change of variables $\zeta=T(\omega-\nu)$ and Plancherel. Thus
$\Phi_{T,\omega}$ is an approximate identity centered at $\omega$. Choose
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(I)$ with $\eta\equiv1$ on a smaller neighborhood of
$\omega$. Then
\[
\langle \mu,\Phi_{T,\omega}\rangle
=\int_{\RR}\eta(\nu)f(\nu)\Phi_{T,\omega}(\nu)\,d\nu
+\langle \mu,(1-\eta)\Phi_{T,\omega}\rangle.
\]
Because $\eta f$ is continuous near $\omega$, the first term tends to
$f(\omega)$. Because $\widehat\chi$ is Schwartz and $(1-\eta)$ vanishes near
$\omega$, the second term tends to $0$ in $\mathcal S(\RR)$. More explicitly,
fix the Schwartz seminorms
\[
p_{m,k}(\psi)=\sup_{\nu\in\RR}(1+|\nu|)^m\bigl|\partial_\nu^k\psi(\nu)\bigr|,
\qquad m,k\in\mathbb N_0.
\]
Choose $\delta>0$ so that $(1-\eta)(\nu)=0$ for $|\nu-\omega|<\delta$. For each
$k$, differentiating $\Phi_{T,\omega}$ gives a finite linear combination of
terms of the form
\[
T^{j+1}
\widehat\chi^{(\ell)}\!\bigl(T(\omega-\nu)\bigr)\,
\overline{\widehat\chi^{(\ell')}\!\bigl(T(\omega-\nu)\bigr)},
\qquad 0\le j,\ell,\ell'\le k.
\]
Hence, on $\operatorname{supp}(1-\eta)$ where $|T(\omega-\nu)|\ge \delta T$,
the Schwartz decay of $\widehat\chi$ implies that for every $L\in\mathbb N$
there is a constant $C_{m,k,L,\eta}$ such that
\[
p_{m,k}\bigl((1-\eta)\Phi_{T,\omega}\bigr)\le C_{m,k,L,\eta}\,T^{-L}.
\]
Thus $(1-\eta)\Phi_{T,\omega}\to0$ in every Schwartz seminorm. Since $\mu$ is a
tempered measure, there exist $C>0$ and finitely many seminorm indices
$(m_r,k_r)$ such that
\[
\bigl|\langle \mu,\psi\rangle\bigr|
\le C\sum_r p_{m_r,k_r}(\psi)
\qquad (\psi\in\mathcal S(\RR)).
\]
Applying this to $\psi=(1-\eta)\Phi_{T,\omega}$ gives
\[
\langle \mu,(1-\eta)\Phi_{T,\omega}\rangle\longrightarrow0.
\]
Therefore
\[
\langle \mu,\Phi_{T,\omega}\rangle\longrightarrow f(\omega).
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{importedinput}[Imported stationary UDW response input at the detector gap, with this paper's normalization]\label{prop:stationary-udw-response-main}
Fix a static worldline through $x$ and a two-level detector with gap $\Omega>0$, coupling scale $\lambda_c$, and fixed spatial profile. Assume \Cref{ass:long-time-switch-main}. In particular, on some open interval containing $\pm\Omega$ the pulled-back spectrum is absolutely continuous with finite continuous density $\widehat W_x$ and has no atom or singular part at $\pm\Omega$. Then the stationary weak-coupling long-time excitation and de-excitation rates are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:long-time-kernel-main}
\frac{1}{T}H_{g\to e}^{(T)}(x,\Omega)
=\lambda_c^2\|\chi\|_2^2\,\langle \widehat W_x,\Phi_{T,\Omega}\rangle,
\qquad
\frac{1}{T}H_{e\to g}^{(T)}(x,\Omega)
=\lambda_c^2\|\chi\|_2^2\,\langle \widehat W_x,\Phi_{T,-\Omega}\rangle,
\end{equation}
where $\Phi_{T,\omega}$ is the approximate-identity family from
\eqref{eq:approx-identity-main}. Since the spectral measure is gap-regular and
absolutely continuous at $\pm\Omega$, with no atom or singular part there,
\Cref{lem:gap-regular-approx-identity-main} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:long-time-limit-main}
\begin{aligned}
\Gamma_+(x,\Omega)
&:=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}H_{g\to e}^{(T)}(x,\Omega)
=\lambda_c^2\|\chi\|_2^2\,\widehat W_x(\Omega),\\
\Gamma_-(x,\Omega)
&:=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}H_{e\to g}^{(T)}(x,\Omega)
=\lambda_c^2\|\chi\|_2^2\,\widehat W_x(-\Omega).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Hence, with
\[
\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2=\lambda_c^2\|\chi\|_2^2,
\]
one obtains
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fourier-rates-main}
\Gamma_+(x,\Omega)=\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\widehat W_x(\Omega),
\qquad
\Gamma_-(x,\Omega)=\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\widehat W_x(-\Omega).
\end{equation}
Thus the long-time rate is obtained by extracting the absolutely continuous
spectral density at the detector gap; it is not a formal evaluation of a
distribution at $\nu=\pm\Omega$.
The detector-response statement is the standard stationary UDW response theorem
with smooth switching and finite-size regularization, in the form used for
stationary trajectories by Letaw and by the later Schlicht--Satz--Louko--Satz
regularization literature \cite{Letaw1981,Schlicht2004,Satz2007,LoukoSatz2006,LoukoSatz2008,FewsterJuarezLouko2016}; compare in particular the switched response
pairing and transition-rate limit in \cite[Sec.~II]{LoukoSatz2008} and the
spatial-profile regularization in \cite[Sec.~III]{LoukoSatz2006}.
The only work done here is the notation and normalization adaptation from that
cited theorem to the Fourier convention, switching scale, and local
gap-regular absolutely continuous spectral hypothesis used in the fixed-response
locus proposition below.
\end{importedinput}

\begin{proof}
Write
\[
g_T(s)=\int_{\RR}\chi_T(u)\chi_T(u-s)\,du.
\]
Then \Cref{ass:long-time-switch-main}(ii) gives
\[
H_{g\to e}^{(T)}(x,\Omega)=\lambda_c^2\langle W_x,e^{-i\Omega(\cdot)}g_T\rangle.
\]
Because $g_T$ is the autocorrelation of $\chi_T$, its Fourier transform is
\[
\widehat g_T(\nu)=|\widehat{\chi_T}(\nu)|^2
=T^2\bigl|\widehat\chi(T\nu)\bigr|^2.
\]
Using the Fourier inversion convention
\[
g(s)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\RR}e^{i\nu s}\widehat g(\nu)\,d\nu,
\]
we obtain the exact spectral representation
\[
\frac{1}{T}H_{g\to e}^{(T)}(x,\Omega)
=\frac{\lambda_c^2}{2\pi T}
\left\langle \widehat W_x,\bigl|\widehat{\chi_T}(\Omega-\cdot)\bigr|^2\right\rangle
=\lambda_c^2\|\chi\|_2^2\,\langle \widehat W_x,\Phi_{T,\Omega}\rangle,
\]
which is \eqref{eq:long-time-kernel-main}; the de-excitation formula is the same
with $\Omega$ replaced by $-\Omega$.
\Cref{lem:gap-regular-approx-identity-main} applied to the positive tempered
spectral measure $\mu_x$ at $\omega=\Omega$ and $\omega=-\Omega$ yields
\eqref{eq:long-time-limit-main}, and therefore
\eqref{eq:fourier-rates-main}. This is the exact long-time normalization used in
the standard smooth-switching stationary detector theorem
\cite[Sec.~II]{LoukoSatz2008}; the later long-waiting-time stationary analysis
of \cite{FewsterJuarezLouko2016} uses the same response-function input.
The proof is included only to fix conventions and the local gap-regular
interface used later.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Local KMS spectral relation near the detector gap, with cited strip input]\label{lem:local-kms-spectral-main}
Assume \Cref{ass:long-time-switch-main}, let the state be $\beta_\infty$-KMS
with respect to static Killing time, and abbreviate
\[
\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}=\beta_\infty N(x).
\]
Let $I\subset I_x$ be any open interval containing $\pm\Omega$. Then for every
$\phi\in C_c^\infty(I)$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:kms-spectral-distribution-main}
\langle \widehat W_x,\phi\rangle
=\left\langle \widehat W_x(-\cdot),
e^{-\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}(\cdot)}\phi(\cdot)\right\rangle.
\end{equation}
If, moreover, $\widehat W_x$ is represented by a continuous density on a
neighborhood of $\pm\Omega$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:kms-detailed-balance-main}
\widehat W_x(-\Omega)=e^{\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}\Omega}\widehat W_x(\Omega).
\end{equation}
This is the usual KMS spectral detailed-balance boundary-value relation,
localized to the detector gap and written in the Fourier convention of this
paper \cite{HaagHugenholtzWinnink1967,KayWald1991,BratteliRobinson1997}.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $\phi\in C_c^\infty(I)$. Define the entire function
\[
h_\phi(z)=\int_{\RR}e^{-i\nu z}\phi(\nu)\,d\nu.
\]
Because $\phi$ has compact support, $h_\phi$ decays faster than any inverse power uniformly on closed horizontal strips. Together with the polynomial bounds in \Cref{ass:long-time-switch-main}(iii), Cauchy's theorem on rectangles in $S_{\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}}^-$ shows that
\[
\int_{\RR}F_x(s-i\eta)\,h_\phi(s-i\eta)\,ds
\]
is independent of $\eta\in(0,\beta_{\mathrm{loc}})$. Taking $\eta\downarrow0$ and $\eta\uparrow\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}$, and using the distributional boundary values from \Cref{ass:long-time-switch-main}(iii), yields
\[
\langle W_x,h_\phi\rangle
=
\langle W_x(-\cdot),h_\phi(\cdot-i\beta_{\mathrm{loc}})\rangle.
\]
Since
\[
h_\phi(s-i\beta_{\mathrm{loc}})
=\int_{\RR}e^{-i\nu s}e^{-\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}\nu}\phi(\nu)\,d\nu
=h_{e^{-\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}(\cdot)}\phi}(s),
\]
the preceding identity becomes
\[
\langle \widehat W_x,\phi\rangle
=
\langle \widehat{W_x(-\cdot)},e^{-\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}(\cdot)}\phi\rangle.
\]
Using $\widehat{W_x(-\cdot)}(\nu)=\widehat W_x(-\nu)$ distributionally, we obtain
\[
\langle \widehat W_x,\phi\rangle
=
\langle e^{-\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}(\cdot)}\widehat W_x(-\cdot),\phi\rangle
\]
for all $\phi\in C_c^\infty(I)$, which is exactly
\eqref{eq:kms-spectral-distribution-main}. If $\widehat W_x$ is represented by
continuous densities on a neighborhood of $\pm\Omega$, choose a standard
approximate delta family $(\phi_\epsilon)_{\epsilon>0}\subset C_c^\infty(I)$
with $\operatorname{supp}\phi_\epsilon\to\{\Omega\}$. Then
\eqref{eq:kms-spectral-distribution-main} gives
\[
\int \widehat W_x(\nu)\phi_\epsilon(\nu)\,d\nu
=
\int \widehat W_x(-\nu)e^{-\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}\nu}\phi_\epsilon(\nu)\,d\nu.
\]
Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ and using continuity at $\pm\Omega$ yields
\eqref{eq:kms-detailed-balance-main}. For operator-algebraic formulations of
the same KMS strip and spectral relation, see
\cite{HaagHugenholtzWinnink1967,KayWald1991,BratteliRobinson1997}.
\end{proof}

Combining \eqref{eq:fourier-rates-main} with
\Cref{lem:local-kms-spectral-main} gives the one-gap detailed-balance ratio
\[
\frac{\Gamma_-(x,\Omega)}{\Gamma_+(x,\Omega)}
=e^{\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}\Omega},
\]
with our convention that $\Gamma_+$ is excitation and $\Gamma_-$ is
de-excitation. If, moreover, the one-gap density is strictly positive,
$\widehat W_x(\Omega)>0$, define the positive spectral weight
\begin{equation}\label{eq:spectral-weight-def-main}
\mathcal S_x(\Omega)=
\bigl(e^{\beta_\infty N(x)\Omega}-1\bigr)\widehat W_x(\Omega).
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:kms-rate-main}
\Gamma_+(x,\Omega)=
\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\,
\frac{\mathcal S_x(\Omega)}{e^{\beta_\infty N(x)\Omega}-1},
\qquad
\Gamma_-(x,\Omega)=
\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\,
\frac{e^{\beta_\infty N(x)\Omega}\mathcal S_x(\Omega)}
{e^{\beta_\infty N(x)\Omega}-1}.
\end{equation}

Thus the KMS condition fixes only the detailed-balance ratio above, with our
convention that $\Gamma_+$ is excitation and $\Gamma_-$ is de-excitation. It
does not, by itself, fix the absolute magnitude of the excitation rate. The
remaining positive factor is a local response spectral weight. We therefore
keep a separate regularity and calibration hypothesis for this factor rather
than treating it as a geometric identity.

\begin{assumption}[Static response regularity and calibration]\label{ass:kms-response-main}
Fix a static region $U$ and a detector with positive gap $\Omega$ and fixed spatial profile. For each static worldline $x\in U$, use the stationary weak-coupling rates supplied by \Cref{prop:stationary-udw-response-main}. Assume explicitly that the pulled-back spectral measure is gap-regular at $\pm\Omega$: on some open interval containing $\pm\Omega$ it is absolutely continuous with continuous finite density $\widehat W_x$, hence has no atom at $\pm\Omega$, and this one-gap density satisfies
\[
\widehat W_x(\Omega)>0.
\]
Define $\mathcal S_x(\Omega)$ by \eqref{eq:spectral-weight-def-main}. The
response model fixes the positive spectral-weight profile
$x\mapsto\mathcal S_x(\Omega)$ on $U$. Whenever the response-level theorem
chain below is invoked, this calibrated profile is assumed to be $C^1$ on the
relevant region, so that the corresponding fixed response function
\[
R_\Omega(x)=
\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\,
\frac{\mathcal S_x(\Omega)}{e^{\beta_\infty N(x)\Omega}-1}
\]
is a positive $C^1$ function there.
\end{assumption}

\begin{proposition}[Boundary example: exact homogeneous amplitude from spatial symmetry]\label{prop:symmetry-homogeneous-main}
Assume, in addition to \Cref{ass:long-time-switch-main}, that the static region is an ultrastatic spacetime $(\mathbb R\times\Sigma,-dt^2+h)$ and that a group $G$ of spatial isometries acts transitively on a region $U\subset\Sigma$. Suppose the $\beta_\infty$-KMS state $\omega$ is invariant under the induced automorphisms $\alpha_g$ of the field algebra, and that the detector profile at $x=gx_0$ is obtained from one reference profile by rigid transport under $g$. Then
\[
W_x(s)=W_{x_0}(s),\qquad
\widehat W_x(\nu)=\widehat W_{x_0}(\nu),\qquad
\mathcal S_x(\Omega)=\mathcal S_{x_0}(\Omega)
\]
for all $x\in U$. Hence the homogeneous spectral-weight regime holds exactly on $U$.

In particular, for a thermal Klein--Gordon KMS state in Minkowski space with identical translated compactly supported smearing profiles, the one-gap spectral weight is exactly independent of the detector position.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let $x=gx_0$ with $g\in G$. By construction of the transported detector profile, the smeared detector observable satisfies
\[
\Phi_x(\tau)=\alpha_g\!\bigl(\Phi_{x_0}(\tau)\bigr).
\]
Using the $G$-invariance of the state,
\[
\begin{aligned}
W_x(s)
&=\omega\!\left(\Phi_x(\tau)\Phi_x(\tau-s)\right) \\
&=\omega\!\left(\alpha_g(\Phi_{x_0}(\tau))\,\alpha_g(\Phi_{x_0}(\tau-s))\right) \\
&=\omega\!\left(\alpha_g(\Phi_{x_0}(\tau)\Phi_{x_0}(\tau-s))\right) \\
&=\omega\!\left(\Phi_{x_0}(\tau)\Phi_{x_0}(\tau-s)\right)
=W_{x_0}(s).
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking Fourier transforms gives $\widehat W_x(\nu)=\widehat W_{x_0}(\nu)$, and then \eqref{eq:spectral-weight-def-main} gives $\mathcal S_x(\Omega)=\mathcal S_{x_0}(\Omega)$. In Minkowski thermal equilibrium the spatial translation group is transitive, the thermal state is translation invariant, and rigidly translated detector profiles satisfy the stated covariance, so the same conclusion applies.
\end{proof}

In this exact symmetry example the ultrastatic lapse satisfies $N\equiv 1$ on
$U$, so the fixed calibrated response function $R_\Omega$ is constant on $U$ as
well. The corresponding level sets are therefore either empty or all of $U$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:symmetry-homogeneous-main} verifies only the homogeneous
amplitude statement $\mathcal S_x(\Omega)\equiv\mathcal S(\Omega)$ in a
constant-lapse symmetry setting; it is not a detector-field construction of
nonconstant-lapse homogeneous shells. Nontrivial homogeneous shell geometry in
the appendices is therefore a separate calibrated response-model hypothesis,
not a consequence of this proposition.

Under \Cref{ass:kms-response-main}, \eqref{eq:kms-rate-main} is used only in the
forward direction needed for shell analysis: a response model fixes the
positive-frequency pullback, then \eqref{eq:spectral-weight-def-main} defines
the spectral weight, and only afterwards are the record-selected target rates
imposed. Read backwards, the same identity merely parametrizes an arbitrary
positive excitation profile with the same detailed-balance ratio:
\[
\mathcal S_x(\Omega)=
\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^{-2}\bigl(e^{\beta_\infty N(x)\Omega}-1\bigr)\Gamma_+(x,\Omega).
\]
Changing that calibrated amplitude changes the response loci while preserving the
one-gap KMS ratio, so from here on we simply freeze the response function
\begin{equation}\label{eq:response-function-main}
R_\Omega(x)=
\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\,
\frac{\mathcal S_x(\Omega)}{e^{\beta_\infty N(x)\Omega}-1}.
\end{equation}
Proposition~\ref{prop:symmetry-homogeneous-main} supplies one exact
detector-field model where the homogeneous specialization
$\mathcal S_x(\Omega)\equiv\mathcal S(\Omega)$ holds, although there the lapse
is constant. The nonconstant-lapse homogeneous case is used only in the
appendices, as abstract calibrated toy-model algebra for this fixed response
function.

\begin{lemma}[One-gap KMS underdetermination]\label{lem:one-gap-kms-underdetermination-main}
At the fixed-gap rate level used in this section, Tolman scaling and KMS detailed balance do not determine the positive excitation-rate profile. Let $G:U\to(0,\infty)$ be any $C^1$ function. The rates
\[
\Gamma_+^G(x,\Omega)=G(x),
\qquad
\Gamma_-^G(x,\Omega)=e^{\beta_\infty N(x)\Omega}G(x)
\]
satisfy the one-gap detailed-balance relation
\[
\Gamma_-^G(x,\Omega)/\Gamma_+^G(x,\Omega)
=e^{\beta_\infty N(x)\Omega},
\]
and can be written in the form \eqref{eq:kms-rate-main} with
\[
\mathcal S_x^G(\Omega)=
\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^{-2}\bigl(e^{\beta_\infty N(x)\Omega}-1\bigr)G(x)>0 .
\]
Consequently, changing the positive spectral weight changes the target-rate loci while preserving the same one-gap detailed-balance ratio. The shell statements below are therefore conditional statements for a fixed response function $R_\Omega$, or for an additional calibration such as the homogeneous spectral-weight regime. This is a fixed-frequency underdetermination statement, not an existence theorem asserting that every such $G$ extends to a global QFT two-point function.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The displayed ratio of $\Gamma_-^G$ and $\Gamma_+^G$ is immediate. Substituting the displayed $\mathcal S_x^G(\Omega)$ into \eqref{eq:kms-rate-main} gives $\Gamma_+^G(x,\Omega)=G(x)$. Since $G$ was arbitrary among positive $C^1$ functions, the equation $G(x)=\gamma$ has whatever regular level-set structure the chosen response profile supplies, subject only to the ordinary range and regularity conditions. Thus detailed balance alone cannot select the shell.
\end{proof}

The underdetermination lemma fixes the logical status of the response profile
before any shell interpretation. Once \eqref{eq:response-function-main} is
fixed, the record analysis supplies two target rates,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:target-rates-main}
\gamma_\varphi=\frac{\log\varphi}{\Delta\tau},
\qquad
\gamma_{\mathrm{mem}}=\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau).
\end{equation}
From this point onward these two symbols are standing shorthand:
$\gamma_\varphi$ and $\gamma_{\mathrm{mem}}$ are not redefined in the later
corollaries, and for $\star\in\{\varphi,\mathrm{mem}\}$ we write
\[
\Sigma_\star^{\mathrm{loc}}:=R_\Omega^{-1}(\gamma_\star)
\]
for the corresponding response locus of the fixed calibrated response function.
The argument from this point onward has three separate layers and we keep
them separate. The classical sampled-counter record law is
\Cref{thm:main-record-wrapper}, with proof components in
\Cref{thm:main-record-wrapper}; the next assumption fixes one stationary response
profile and the sole Model~A calibration bridge; the corollary after the
level-set proposition then turns the two classical thresholds into response loci.
This is the point of the separation: the regular-level-set algebra below is
not a new detector-dynamics theorem.  Rigorous UDW foundations, including the
joint interacting Hilbert-space status of UDW-type models, are treated in the
recent detector literature \cite{TjoaGray2024UDWJointHilbert}; here that
literature is used only as a boundary reference because the proposition below
assumes a calibrated response profile and applies the ordinary level-set
theorem.

\begin{assumption}[Model A: sampled counter with one fixed response closure]\label{ass:udw-rate-calibration-main}
\leavevmode\par\smallskip
\noindent\fbox{%
\parbox{\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax}{%
\textbf{Model A.}
Sections~\ref{sec:operational}--\ref{sec:records} have already fixed one
classical sampled counter law. In the response layer we do not derive that
counter law from KMS thermality or from general UDW measurement dynamics.
Instead, we fix one stationary detector response profile and impose only the
closure
\[
\Gamma=R_\Omega(x)=\Gamma_+(x,\Omega).
\]
All response loci, shell upgrades, transport identities, and inverse
corollaries below are conditional consequences of that prescribed calibration
step.
}}

Work under \Cref{ass:kms-response-main}. Fix a detector gap $\Omega>0$ and a
static region $U$. The stationary detector response calculation may motivate
the following scalar profile, but Model~A treats it as externally supplied
calibration data: one positive $C^1$ function
\[
R_\Omega:U\to(0,\infty),
\qquad
R_\Omega(x)=\Gamma_+(x,\Omega)
=\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\,
\frac{\mathcal S_x(\Omega)}{e^{\beta_\infty N(x)\Omega}-1}.
\]
Once this function is fixed, the remaining analysis in this section is level-
set algebra for that one prescribed response profile, exactly as stipulated in
Model~A.
\end{assumption}

\begin{assumption}[Standing response-side hypotheses for the fixed-response results]\label{ass:response-standing-main}
Work under \Cref{ass:udw-rate-calibration-main}. Thus one fixed static region
$U$, one detector gap $\Omega>0$, and one calibrated response profile
$R_\Omega:U\to(0,\infty)$ have already been chosen. In particular:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.2em,itemsep=0.25em]
\item for every static worldline $x\in U$, the pulled-back spectral measure is
gap-regular at $\pm\Omega$, absolutely continuous with continuous finite
density $\widehat W_x$ on a neighborhood of $\pm\Omega$, and has no atom or
singular part there;
\item the positive-frequency density satisfies $\widehat W_x(\Omega)>0$ on $U$;
\item the calibrated spectral weight
$x\mapsto\mathcal S_x(\Omega)$ is a positive $C^1$ function on $U$;
\item equivalently, the fixed response profile
\[
R_\Omega(x)=
\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\,
\frac{\mathcal S_x(\Omega)}{e^{\beta_\infty N(x)\Omega}-1}
\]
is a positive $C^1$ function on $U$.
\end{enumerate}
Every result below about this response profile, its level sets, transport
identities, or fixed-radius inverse statements is read inside this standing
hypothesis package unless it explicitly adds a stronger specialization, such
as homogeneous spectral weight, a small-locus horizon family, or externally
supplied ratio-data asymptotics.
\end{assumption}

The next proposition is therefore only about level sets of one fixed calibrated
response function.

\begin{proposition}[Fixed-response locus theorem for one calibrated response function]\label{thm:response-locus-main}
\ResponseStandingClause let $\gamma>0$ be any target
rate, and define
\[
L_\gamma=\{x\in U:R_\Omega(x)=\gamma\}.
\]
Then $L_\gamma$ is empty exactly when $\gamma$ lies outside the range of
$R_\Omega$ on $U$. If $x_0\in L_\gamma$ and $dR_\Omega(x_0)\neq 0$, then
$L_\gamma$ is, near $x_0$, a $C^1$ codimension-one hypersurface with normal
covector $dR_\Omega(x_0)$.
No detector-dynamics or UDW Hilbert-space theorem is claimed here: the detector
model has already entered only through the fixed calibrated function
$R_\Omega$. If $dR_\Omega(x_0)=0$, this proposition draws no conclusion and asserts
no converse to the regular-level-set criterion.

In the calibrated homogeneous spectral-weight regime,
$\mathcal S_x(\Omega)\equiv\mathcal S(\Omega)$, the equation $R_\Omega(x)=\gamma$
is equivalent to
\[
\beta_\infty N(x)=\beta_\gamma,
\qquad
\beta_\gamma=\frac{1}{\Omega}
\log\!\left(1+\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\mathcal S(\Omega)}{\gamma}\right).
\]
In that regime $dR_\Omega(x_0)\neq 0$ if and only if $dN(x_0)\neq0$. Only after
the target has passed the range check
$\gamma\in\operatorname{range}(R_\Omega)$ and a chosen component has passed the
regularity check $dR_\Omega(x_0)\neq 0$ may that component be described as a
regular codimension-one shell in the spatial static model.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The first assertion is the definition of the range. The local hypersurface
statement is the regular level-set theorem applied to the $C^1$ function
$R_\Omega$. These two steps exhaust the proposition's dynamical content: all
detector and field dynamics have already been compressed into the prescribed
calibrated response profile by \Cref{ass:udw-rate-calibration-main}.

If $\mathcal S_x(\Omega)$ is constant, the equation
\[
\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\frac{\mathcal S(\Omega)}{e^{\beta_\infty N(x)\Omega}-1}=\gamma
\]
is equivalent to
\[
e^{\beta_\infty N(x)\Omega}
=1+\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\mathcal S(\Omega)}{\gamma},
\]
which gives the displayed value of $\beta_\gamma$. Differentiating the
homogeneous response function gives
\[
dR_\Omega
=
-\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\mathcal S(\Omega)
\frac{\beta_\infty\Omega e^{\beta_\infty N\Omega}}
{(e^{\beta_\infty N\Omega}-1)^2}\,dN .
\]
The scalar prefactor is strictly negative on $U$, so $dR_\Omega(x_0)$
vanishes exactly when $dN(x_0)$ vanishes.
\end{proof}

Under \Cref{ass:udw-rate-calibration-main}, the two classical target rates from
\Cref{sec:records} now select the response-level equations
\[
\Gamma=R_\Omega(x)=\gamma_\varphi,
\qquad
\Gamma=R_\Omega(x)=\gamma_{\mathrm{mem}}.
\]
Those equations remain only target substitutions inside the fixed calibrated
response model until the range and regularity checks from
\Cref{thm:response-locus-main} are verified. Appendix
~\ref{app:abstract-homogeneous-main} records the corresponding threshold
substitutions as conditional corollaries: first the two response loci
selected by $\gamma_\varphi$ and $\gamma_{\mathrm{mem}}$, then the later
homogeneous toy-model algebra built on top of those loci. Thus
\Cref{lem:one-gap-kms-underdetermination-main,ass:udw-rate-calibration-main,thm:response-locus-main}
remain the entire bridge from record thresholds to response-locus language:
calibration dependence first, fixed-response closure second, regular level
sets third, and shell terminology only after the checks inside
\Cref{thm:response-locus-main}. The nonconstant-lapse homogeneous shell
specializations, quotient laws, near-horizon limits, fixed-radius
inverse/admissibility statements, and Schwarzschild insertions are kept out of
the main text and collected instead in the abstract calibrated toy-model
Appendices~\ref{app:abstract-homogeneous-main} and~\ref{sec:inverse},
together with Appendix~\ref{app:schwarzschild-toy}.

\section{Record, inverse, and finite-record results}\label{sec:records}

This section gives the record-side results in compressed form.  Each main
result is read under the constrained D-MAP record assumption
\Cref{ass:model-inference-contract-main}, with any extra regularity or
finite-record protocol stated locally.  Between those statements, all
probabilities below are probabilities of the stationary visible binary record
generated by the sampled-counter labelled kernels \(T_0,T_1\).
The killed entries \(T_1(R,R)=T_1(D,R)=0\) are used as assumptions, not as
conclusions; \Cref{prop:model-fragility-boundary-reset-main} states exactly
which renewal and inverse conclusions are lost for same-bin recovery leakage.
Throughout this section \((A_n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}\) denotes that two-sided
stationary extension.
One-sided strings such as \(A_0,\ldots,A_{N-1}\) are finite restrictions used
only for observed-record statistics; when a proof conditions on a past event
or shifts a renewal epoch, it is using the same stationary two-sided process.

\subsection{Model and renewal law}

\begin{proposition}[Constrained D-MAP labelled kernels]\label{prop:instrument-kernels-main}
Fix \(\Gamma,\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau>0\).  With hidden states ordered as
\((R,D)\), let
\begin{equation}\label{eq:t0-t1-main}
T_0=
\begin{pmatrix}
p&0\\ b&s
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
T_1=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&1-p\\0&a
\end{pmatrix},
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:p-c-main}
p=e^{-\Gamma\Delta\tau},
\qquad
s=e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm r}\Delta\tau},
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:a-b-main}
a=\int_0^{\Delta\tau}\kappa_{\mathrm r}e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm r}r}
\bigl(1-e^{-\Gamma(\Delta\tau-r)}\bigr)\,dr,
\qquad
b=\int_0^{\Delta\tau}\kappa_{\mathrm r}e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm r}r}
e^{-\Gamma(\Delta\tau-r)}\,dr .
\end{equation}
For \(\kappa_{\mathrm r}\ne\Gamma\),
\[
a=\frac{\kappa_{\mathrm r}(1-p)-\Gamma(1-s)}
        {\kappa_{\mathrm r}-\Gamma},
\qquad
b=\frac{\kappa_{\mathrm r}(p-s)}
        {\kappa_{\mathrm r}-\Gamma},
\]
with continuous equal-rate limits.  The labelled-kernel convention is
\((T_i)_{XY}=\PP(A_n=i,H_{n+1}=Y\mid H_n=X)\), and word probabilities are
\(\pi T_{u_0}\cdots T_{u_{m-1}}\mathbf1\) from the stationary hidden law.
These are the kernels fixed in \Cref{ass:model-inference-contract-main}.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The two rows define a labelled transition kernel directly.  From state \(R\),
the zero-labelled transition remains in \(R\) with probability \(p\), while the
one-labelled transition goes to \(D\) with probability \(1-p\).  From state
\(D\), the zero-labelled transition has weights \(b\) to \(R\) and \(s\) to
\(D\), and the one-labelled transition has weight \(a\) to \(D\).  The
integrals define nonnegative weights with \(a+b=1-s\), so the two row sums of
\(T_0+T_1\) are one.  Thus \(T_0,T_1\) form the stated D-MAP kernels.  The
displayed unequal-rate formulas are the elementary evaluations of the two
integrals, with continuous limits on the equal-rate diagonal.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Equal-rate and critical notation]\label{lem:equal-rate-critical-convention-main}
The survival factors are always
\[
p=e^{-\Gamma\Delta\tau},\qquad
s=e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm r}\Delta\tau},
\]
and throughout the stipulated-kernel algebra
\[
q=1-p .
\]
The hidden eigenvalue is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:lambda-hid-main}
\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}
=p-b
=\frac{\kappa_{\mathrm r}s-\Gamma p}{\kappa_{\mathrm r}-\Gamma}
\quad(\kappa_{\mathrm r}\ne\Gamma),
\end{equation}
with continuous equal-rate value
\(\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}=e^{-y}(1-y)\), where
\(y=\kappa_{\mathrm r}\Delta\tau=\Gamma\Delta\tau\) on the equal-rate
diagonal.  Put
\[
x=\Gamma\Delta\tau,\qquad y=\kappa_{\mathrm r}\Delta\tau .
\]
For \(x\ne y\),
\[
\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x e^{-x}=y e^{-y}.
\]
The equation \(x e^{-x}=y e^{-y}\) always has the formal solution \(x=y\).
For \(y\ne1\) this diagonal solution is only the removable zero of the
multiplied quotient numerator, not a zero of the continuous eigenvalue
\(\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}\).  The critical rate is therefore the non-removable
branch
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gamma-crit-piecewise-main}
\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau)
=\Delta\tau^{-1}
\begin{cases}
x_+(y),&0<y<1,\quad x_+(y)>1,\quad x_+(y)e^{-x_+(y)}=y e^{-y},\\
1,&y=1,\\
x_-(y),&y>1,\quad 0<x_-(y)<1,\quad x_-(y)e^{-x_-(y)}=y e^{-y}.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
Equivalently, for \(y\ne1\) it is the unique positive solution of
\(x e^{-x}=y e^{-y}\) on the opposite side of \(1\) from \(y\), and the
removable equal-rate branch \(x=y\) is explicitly excluded.  Only at \(y=1\)
does the equal-rate branch become a genuine zero, giving
\(\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}=\kappa_{\mathrm r}=1/\Delta\tau\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The identity \(p-b\) and the quotient form follow from
\eqref{eq:a-b-main}.  The equal-rate value is l'Hopital's rule, equivalently
\(b=y e^{-y}\) when \(\kappa_{\mathrm r}=\Gamma\), and hence
\(\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}=e^{-y}(1-y)\).  For \(x\ne y\), multiplying the
quotient numerator by \(\Delta\tau\) gives the scalar equation
\(x e^{-x}=y e^{-y}\).  The function \(x\mapsto xe^{-x}\) is strictly
increasing on \((0,1)\), strictly decreasing on \((1,\infty)\), and has its
only maximum at \(1\).  Hence the level through \(y\ne1\) has exactly one
positive solution on the opposite side of \(1\), in addition to the removable
solution \(x=y\).  This gives the two non-removable branches in
\eqref{eq:gamma-crit-piecewise-main}.  When \(y=1\), the opposite branch
coalesces with the diagonal and the equal-rate limit \(e^{-1}(1-1)=0\) gives
\(\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}=1/\Delta\tau=\kappa_{\mathrm r}\).
\end{proof}

For later audits, the equal-rate diagonal
\(\Gamma=\kappa_{\mathrm r}\), \(y=\Gamma\Delta\tau\), \(p=e^{-y}\), is
summarized by the single dictionary
\begin{equation}\label{eq:equal-rate-dictionary-main}
\begin{aligned}
a&=1-(1+y)p,&
b&=yp,\\
\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}&=p-b=(1-y)p,&
S_k&=\PP(G\ge k)=p^k(1+yk),\\
g_k&=p^k\bigl((1-p)(1+yk)-yp\bigr),&
h_k&=\frac{(1-p)+y(k(1-p)-p)}{1+yk},
\qquad k\ge0 .
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Regeneration and zero-run law]\label{lem:renewal-gap-main}
Let \(G\) be the number of zeros between consecutive clicks in the stationary
constrained D-MAP record.  Click times are regeneration times.  For
\(k\ge0\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gap-main}
g_k=\PP(G=k)=e_D^\top T_0^kT_1\mathbf1 .
\end{equation}
If \(\kappa_{\mathrm r}\ne\Gamma\), then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gap-closed-main}
g_k=
\frac{\kappa_{\mathrm r}(1-p)p^k-\Gamma(1-s)s^k}
     {\kappa_{\mathrm r}-\Gamma}.
\end{equation}
The gap law has full support on \(\mathbb N_0\) and an exponential tail.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
After a click the next hidden state is \(D\), independently of the earlier
record.  Thus a gap of \(k\) zeros followed by a click has probability
\eqref{eq:gap-main}.  Since \(T_0\) is lower triangular,
\[
\textstyle\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}s^jp^{k-1-j}=0\quad(k=0),
\]
with the displayed sum interpreted as empty when \(k=0\), and
\[
T_0^k=
\begin{pmatrix}
p^k&0\\
b\textstyle\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}s^jp^{k-1-j}&s^k
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Therefore
\[
e_D^\top T_0^kT_1\mathbf1
=b(1-p)\textstyle\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}s^jp^{k-1-j}+as^k,
\]
where the comma only separates the display from the following substitution.
For \(p\ne s\),
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}s^jp^{k-1-j}=\frac{p^k-s^k}{p-s}.
\]
Substituting
\[
a=\frac{\kappa_{\mathrm r}(1-p)-\Gamma(1-s)}
        {\kappa_{\mathrm r}-\Gamma},
\qquad
b=\frac{\kappa_{\mathrm r}(p-s)}
        {\kappa_{\mathrm r}-\Gamma}
\]
therefore gives
\[
b(1-p)\frac{p^k-s^k}{p-s}+as^k
=
\frac{\kappa_{\mathrm r}(1-p)p^k-\Gamma(1-s)s^k}
     {\kappa_{\mathrm r}-\Gamma},
\]
which is \eqref{eq:gap-closed-main}.  If \(p=s\), equivalently
\(\kappa_{\mathrm r}=\Gamma\), the same identity is read by the continuous
equal-rate dictionary \eqref{eq:equal-rate-dictionary-main}.  All terms are
probabilities of disjoint paths, so they are positive, and the two survival
factors lie in \((0,1)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Support of finite binary words]\label{cor:word-support-main}
Every finite binary word has positive probability under the stationary
constrained D-MAP record.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Let the word be \(w=(w_0,\ldots,w_{m-1})\), with \(m\ge1\), and write
\[
S=\{i\in\{0,\ldots,m-1\}:w_i=1\}.
\]
We work in the two-sided stationary renewal click set
\(\varXi=\{n:A_n=1\}\).  Embed the observed window in the longer interval
\([-1,m]\) and force clicks at both artificial endpoints.  More explicitly,
list the finite set
\[
C=\{-1\}\cup S\cup\{m\}=\{c_0<c_1<\cdots<c_J\}.
\]
Consider the event that \(c_0,c_1,\ldots,c_J\) are consecutive renewal
clicks, with no further clicks between them.  Under the stationary law this
event has probability
\[
\PP(c_0\in\varXi)\prod_{j=0}^{J-1}
\PP\bigl(G=c_{j+1}-c_j-1\bigr)
=\rho\prod_{j=0}^{J-1}g_{c_{j+1}-c_j-1}.
\]
Each displayed gap length is a nonnegative integer, including at the two
observed-window boundaries.  By \Cref{lem:renewal-gap-main},
\(\rho>0\) and \(g_k>0\) for every \(k\ge0\), so the event has positive
probability.  On this event the restriction of the click set to
\(\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\) is exactly \(S\): the forced interior clicks are precisely
the one-sites of \(w\), and the ``consecutive clicks'' condition rules out
clicks at every zero-site.  Hence the cylinder probability of \(w\) is at
least this positive probability.  The empty word has probability \(1\).
\end{proof}

\subsection{Exact dependence, hazard, and count diagnostics}

These are falsification diagnostics only; no size, power, or post-selection
coverage theorem is proved for these diagnostics.
The hazard, Fano, and low-lag formulas in this subsection have the inferential
status fixed in \Cref{ass:model-inference-contract-main}.  The hazard,
spectral-density, and Fano displays in this subsection are population
identities or inputs to later sandwich/projection procedures.

\begin{lemma}[Stationary hidden law]\label{lem:stationary-main}
For \(P=T_0+T_1=\begin{psmallmatrix}p&q\\ b&1-b\end{psmallmatrix}\), the
stationary hidden law is
\[
\pi=\left(\frac b{q+b},\frac{q}{q+b}\right).
\]
With \(q=1-p\) as fixed in \Cref{lem:equal-rate-critical-convention-main}, the
stationary click density is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rho-main}
\rho=\pi T_1\mathbf1=\frac{q(1-s)}{q+b}.
\end{equation}
Moreover \(a<q(1-s)<q\), and therefore
\(a-\rho=-b(q-a)/(q+b)<0\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Solving \(\pi P=\pi\) gives the displayed law.  Since
\(u=T_1\mathbf1=(q,a)^\top\) and \(a+b=1-s\), \(\rho=\pi u\) gives
\eqref{eq:rho-main}.  For \(r>0\),
\[
1-e^{-\Gamma(\Delta\tau-r)}<1-e^{-\Gamma\Delta\tau}=q,
\]
so the defining integral for \(a\) gives
\[
a<q\int_0^{\Delta\tau}\kappa_{\mathrm r}e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm r}r}\,dr
=q(1-s)<q .
\]
The sign follows from
\[
a-\rho=-\frac{b(q-a)}{q+b}
\]
and the strict positivity of \(b\) and \(q-a\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Covariance transfer through the hidden mode]\label{lem:covariance-transfer-main}
For the stationary D-MAP record,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cov-transfer-main}
\PP(A_n=1\mid A_0=1)
=\rho+(a-\rho)\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}^{\,n-1},
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(A_0,A_n)=\rho(a-\rho)\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}^{\,n-1}
\end{equation}
for \(n\ge1\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
With \(q=1-p\) and \(u=(q,a)^\top\),
\[
u-\rho\mathbf1=\frac{q-a}{q+b}\binom {q}{-b},
\qquad
P\binom {q}{-b}=(p-b)\binom {q}{-b}.
\]
Thus
\[
P^{n-1}u=\rho\mathbf1+
\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}^{n-1}(u-\rho\mathbf1).
\]
A click at time \(0\) sets the next hidden state to \(D\).  Hence
\[
\PP(A_n=1\mid A_0=1)
=e_D^\top P^{n-1}u
=\rho+\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}^{n-1}(a-\rho),
\]
because the \(D\)-component of \(u-\rho\mathbf1\) is \(a-\rho\).  Multiplying
by \(\rho=\PP(A_0=1)\) and subtracting \(\rho^2\) gives the covariance in
\eqref{eq:cov-transfer-main}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Critical-rate uniqueness and covariance phase]\label{lem:critical-rate-main}
For fixed \(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau>0\), the equation
\(\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}(\Gamma)=0\) has the unique positive solution
\(\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau)\) defined by the
piecewise non-removable branch
\eqref{eq:gamma-crit-piecewise-main}.  When
\(\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}\ne\kappa_{\mathrm r}\), this is equivalently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gamma-c-main}
\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}e^{-\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}\Delta\tau}
=\kappa_{\mathrm r}e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm r}\Delta\tau}.
\end{equation}
The displayed scalar equation also has the diagonal solution
\(\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}=\kappa_{\mathrm r}\), but that solution is removable
for \(\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}\) unless
\(\kappa_{\mathrm r}\Delta\tau=1\).  Thus on the diagonal
\(\Gamma=\kappa_{\mathrm r}\), the zero occurs only at
\(\Gamma=\kappa_{\mathrm r}=1/\Delta\tau\).
The sign of \(\operatorname{Cov}(A_0,A_n)\) is the sign of
\(-\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}^{\,n-1}\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The uniqueness is the branch statement in
\Cref{lem:equal-rate-critical-convention-main}.  The covariance sign follows
from \(\rho>0\) and \(a-\rho<0\) in \Cref{lem:stationary-main}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Hidden-mode contraction]\label{lem:hidden-mode-contraction-main}
For every positive constrained D-MAP setting,
\[
|\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}|<1 .
\]
In particular the shifted geometric Fourier series in
\Cref{prop:spectrum-main} is absolutely convergent.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The transition matrix
\[
P=T_0+T_1=
\begin{pmatrix}
p&1-p\\ b&1-b
\end{pmatrix}
\]
is a two-state stochastic matrix with strictly positive off-diagonal entries
\(1-p>0\) and \(b>0\).  Its eigenvalues are \(1\) and
\(\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}=p-b\).  The upper bound is immediate from \(p<1\)
and \(b>0\): \(\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}<1\).  For the lower bound, \(p>0\) and
\[
b=\int_0^{\Delta\tau}\kappa_{\mathrm r}e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm r}r}
e^{-\Gamma(\Delta\tau-r)}\,dr
<\int_0^{\Delta\tau}\kappa_{\mathrm r}e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm r}r}\,dr
=1-s<1 .
\]
Thus \(\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}=p-b>-1\).  Hence
\(|\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}|<1\).  Absolute convergence follows from
\(\sum_{n\ge1}|\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}|^{n-1}<\infty\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Finite hidden-start path-space contraction]\label{lem:finite-hidden-start-path-contraction-main}
Fix one positive constrained D-MAP setting and put \(P=T_0+T_1\).  Let
\(\pi\) be the stationary hidden law.  For a hidden initial law \(\nu\), let
\(\PP_\nu\) denote the one-sided hidden/visible law started from \(H_0\sim\nu\),
and let \(\PP_\pi\) denote the stationary-start law.  There are constants
\(C<\infty\) and \(\theta\in(0,1)\), depending only on the fixed setting, such
that for every burn-in length \(L\ge0\), every retained length \(N\ge1\), and
every set \(B\subset\{0,1\}^N\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:finite-hidden-start-path-tv-main}
\left|
\PP_\nu\bigl((A_L,\ldots,A_{L+N-1})\in B\bigr)
-
\PP_\pi\bigl((A_0,\ldots,A_{N-1})\in B\bigr)
\right|
\le C\theta^L .
\end{equation}
Equivalently,
\[
\sup_{B\subset\{0,1\}^N}
\left|
\PP_\nu\bigl((A_L,\ldots,A_{L+N-1})\in B\bigr)
-
\PP_\pi\bigl((A_0,\ldots,A_{N-1})\in B\bigr)
\right|
\le C\theta^L ,
\]
up to the harmless convention-dependent factor in the definition of total
variation.  The bound is uniform in \(N\).  Consequently, if \(L_N\to\infty\)
and \(S_N\) is any measurable statistic of the retained visible word
\((A_{L_N},\ldots,A_{L_N+N-1})\), then every stationary-start convergence in
distribution, convergence in probability, or event-probability limit for
\(S_N\) transfers unchanged to the finite hidden start.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For a word \(w=(w_0,\ldots,w_{N-1})\), write
\(T_w=T_{w_0}\cdots T_{w_{N-1}}\).  For a set
\(B\subset\{0,1\}^N\), put \(M_B=\sum_{w\in B}T_w\).  Since
\(\sum_{w\in\{0,1\}^N}T_w=P^N\), the matrix \(M_B\) is substochastic: its
entries are nonnegative and \(0\le M_B\mathbf1\le\mathbf1\) coordinatewise.
The retained visible word probability from the finite start is therefore
\[
\PP_\nu\bigl((A_L,\ldots,A_{L+N-1})\in B\bigr)
=\nu P^L M_B\mathbf1,
\]
while stationarity gives
\[
\PP_\pi\bigl((A_0,\ldots,A_{N-1})\in B\bigr)
=\pi M_B\mathbf1 .
\]
Thus the difference is
\[
(\nu P^L-\pi)M_B\mathbf1 .
\]
Because \(0\le M_B\mathbf1\le\mathbf1\), the total-variation dual inequality
gives
\[
\left|(\nu P^L-\pi)M_B\mathbf1\right|
\le \|\nu P^L-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}} .
\]

It remains only to bound the hidden-chain term.  The matrix
\[
P=\begin{pmatrix}p&1-p\\ b&1-b\end{pmatrix}
\]
has strictly positive off-diagonal entries, stationary law
\(\pi=(b/(1-p+b),(1-p)/(1-p+b))\), and nontrivial eigenvalue
\(\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}=p-b\).  By
\Cref{lem:hidden-mode-contraction-main}, \(|\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}|<1\).
On the two-state zero-sum subspace, multiplication by \(P\) is multiplication
by \(\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}\).  Hence, for every initial law \(\nu\),
\[
\|\nu P^L-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\le C|\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}|^L
\]
with a finite constant \(C\) uniform over \(\nu\).  Taking any
\(\theta\in(|\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}|,1)\), or \(\theta=|\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}|\)
when \(\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}\ne0\) and increasing \(C\) if desired, proves
\eqref{eq:finite-hidden-start-path-tv-main}.

The final assertion follows because every statistic of the retained word is a
measurable image of that \(N\)-word.  Total variation cannot increase under a
measurable map, so the law of \(S_N\) under the finite hidden start differs
from its stationary-start law by at most \(C\theta^{L_N}\to0\).  Applying this
bound to continuity sets gives distributional convergence; applying it to the
events \(\{|S_N-s|>\varepsilon\}\), or to the events appearing in a stated
probability limit, gives convergence in probability and event-probability
limits.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Hazard obstruction to finite symbolic memory]\label{lem:hazard-obstruction-main}
A renewal binary process with full gap support is a finite-order Markov chain
only if its gap hazard is eventually constant.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For a renewal process, after observing \(k\) consecutive zeros since the last
click, the conditional click probability is the zero-run hazard \(h_k\).
If an \(r\)-step Markov rule generated the same full-support law, then all
histories with \(k\ge r\) trailing zeros would have the same last \(r\) symbols
and hence the same click probability.  Therefore \(h_k\) would be constant for
all \(k\ge r\).

This condition concerns a transition rule conditioned on the most recent
symbols.  It is different from finite dependence of separated sigma-fields:
\(1\)-dependence says that events separated by one unobserved sample
factorize, while an \(r\)-step Markov rule says that every future one-step
transition probability is a function of only the last \(r\) symbols.  For a
renewal record with full gap support, the latter would force the click
probability after a long zero run to stop depending on the run length.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Cylinder factorization at the memory threshold]\label{lem:kernel-factorization-main}
If \(\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}=0\), then \(P=T_0+T_1=\mathbf1\pi\).  More
explicitly, let \(u=(u_0,\ldots,u_{r-1})\) and
\(v=(v_0,\ldots,v_{\ell-1})\) be arbitrary finite binary words and write
\(T_u=T_{u_0}\cdots T_{u_{r-1}}\), \(T_v=T_{v_0}\cdots T_{v_{\ell-1}}\).
If the word \(u\) is observed on one block and \(v\) is observed on a second
block beginning two samples later, with the intervening sample unobserved,
then
\[
\PP(A_0^{r-1}=u,\ A_{r+1}^{r+\ell}=v)
=\pi T_u P T_v\mathbf1
=\bigl(\pi T_u\mathbf1\bigr)\bigl(\pi T_v\mathbf1\bigr).
\]
Consequently every two visible blocks separated by one unobserved sample are
independent, so the visible record is exact \(1\)-dependent.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The second eigenvalue of \(P\) is \(\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}\), while the first is
\(1\).  At \(\lambda_{\mathrm{hid}}=0\), the primitive stochastic matrix
\(P\) has rank one and both rows equal \(\pi\), hence \(P=\mathbf1\pi\).
For fixed words \(u\) and \(v\), summing over the unobserved sample between
